Chapter 9: Overcoming Obstacles—Navigating Setbacks and Building Resilience.
Every journey, especially when it comes to learning about money, comes with its share of bumps in the road. No one gets it right all the time, and that’s totally normal. Kids and families alike are going to run into things like surprise expenses, the urge to spend more than planned, or feeling let down when reaching a goal takes longer than expected.
So, how do you handle those setbacks? It all starts with patience, openness, and putting the spotlight on resilience.
Here’s something that can really change the way you see obstacles—what if you started looking at them as opportunities to grow?
Take this for example: if your child spends all their savings on something impulsively, it’s not just a mistake. It’s actually a perfect moment to pause, talk about what happened, and brainstorm together about how to plan differently next time. Or maybe your family is hit with an unexpected financial setback. Involving your kids in simple, age-appropriate conversations about how you might adjust your goals or priorities can actually build trust and help them become better problem solvers.
There are a few gentle strategies that can help everyone navigate these rough patches:
First, normalize mistakes. Let your children—and yourself—know that everyone slips up with money sometimes. What really matters is what you learn and how you move forward from it.
Second, reflect together. After something doesn’t go as planned, just sit down and talk about it. Ask what happened, share how everyone felt, and think about what you might try differently next time.
And third, don’t be afraid to adjust your goals when life changes. Maybe you need to tweak the timeline or the target. That’s not a sign of failure—it’s actually a sign of flexibility and strength.
Here’s another thing worth celebrating: persistence. When your child keeps saving after a disappointment, or your family sticks with a giving goal even when it’s tough, that’s a huge win. These moments, even if they feel small, build up confidence and a real sense of agency over time.
It also helps to keep your focus on values, not just outcomes. Let’s say you set a goal to give, but you don’t reach it. The effort and intention matter just as much as the final result. And if saving takes longer than you hoped, remember—having the habit of putting money aside is a success all on its own.
So, what’s the big takeaway here? Overcoming obstacles is just part of the money journey. When you approach setbacks with compassion and a growth mindset, your family—and your kids—will build resilience, adaptability, and the confidence to keep moving forward, no matter what comes your way.
